balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Thales SA: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Thales SA: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For Thales SA: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Thales SA: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Thales SA: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Thales SA: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Thales SA: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Thales SA: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Thales SA: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

segmentRevenue.title: Revenue by segment
segmentRevenue.content:
Thales reports three segments: Aerospace (avionics, in-flight entertainment, space), Defence & Security (land/air/naval defence systems, cybersecurity for government), and Digital Identity & Security (biometrics, payment cards, IoT security -- including the former Gemalto/Thales DIS business).

For Thales SA: Defence & Security is the growth engine behind European rearmament, up from €9.16bn to €12.23bn FY2022-FY2025 (+33.6%), while Digital Identity & Security has been choppier (€3.62bn → €4.02bn → €3.85bn) and Aerospace is recovering post-COVID air-traffic recovery.

What to watch:

  • Defence's share of group revenue rising as rearmament budgets scale
  • Whether Digital Identity & Security stabilises or keeps lagging

segmentEbit.title: Adjusted EBIT by segment
segmentEbit.content:
Segment-level adjusted EBIT is operating profitability before one-offs and PPA amortisation, allocated to each of the three segments -- the margin counterpart to the revenue split above.

For Thales SA: Defence & Security's adjusted EBIT grew faster than its revenue (€1,179m → €1,619m, +37.3% FY2022-FY2025), evidence of operating leverage on the rearmament ramp. Digital Identity & Security's EBIT fell in FY2025 (€585m → €526m) even as the segment is smaller than Defence, the clearest sign of margin pressure in that business.

What to watch:

  • Defence margin expansion continuing as volume scales
  • Whether Digital Identity & Security's EBIT decline is cyclical or structural

segmentOrderBook.title: Order book by segment
segmentOrderBook.content:
The order book is unfulfilled signed contracts -- future revenue already booked. Thales discloses it for Aerospace and Defence & Security; Digital Identity & Security does not report a comparable backlog.

For Thales SA: Defence & Security's order book is nearly 4x Aerospace's (€41.6bn vs €10.8bn at FY2025) and has grown every year since FY2022 (€31.0bn → €41.6bn), the clearest forward-looking evidence that European rearmament is being converted into multi-year contracted revenue rather than just headline order intake.

What to watch:

  • Order book growing faster than revenue (book-to-bill above 1x)
  • Concentration risk in large multi-year defence programmes

segmentOrderIntake.title: Order intake by segment
segmentOrderIntake.content:
Order intake is new contracts signed in the period -- the flow that builds the order book shown above.

For Thales SA: Defence & Security order intake has risen every year (€13.96bn FY2022 → €15.13bn FY2025), consistent with European governments committing new defence budgets. Aerospace intake is more cyclical, tracking aircraft order cycles (€5.89bn → €6.43bn → €6.12bn).

What to watch:

  • Intake outpacing revenue (expanding the order book) versus merely replacing it
  • Lumpiness from single large contract wins in any one year

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Thales SA: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
